node.label: Barbara J. Fields
node.date_label: “Ideology and Race” (1982) · Slavery and Freedom on the Middle Ground (1985) · “Slavery, Race and Ideology” (1990) · Slaves No More, coauthor (1992) · Racecraft, with Karen E. Fields (2012)
node.description: In Racecraft: The Soul of Inequality in American Life (2012), Barbara J. Fields and Karen E. Fields argue that the practice of racism produces the illusion of race. They call the process that produces this illusion “racecraft.” Barbara Fields’s “Slavery, Race and Ideology in the United States of America” (1990) criticizes treating American slavery primarily as a system of race relations and rejects the biological reality of race. Her work also includes the Maryland study Slavery and Freedom on the Middle Ground (1985) and the collaborative emancipation history Slaves No More (1992). Walter Johnson’s “Brute Ideology” (2014) praised Racecraft’s analysis while questioning its narrow textual remedy and treatment of resistant political cultures.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Ideology and Race in American History” (1982); Slavery and Freedom on the Middle Ground: Maryland during the Nineteenth Century (1985); “Slavery, Race and Ideology in the United States of America” (1990); Slaves No More (1992), with Ira Berlin, Steven F. Miller, Joseph P. Reidy and Leslie S. Rowland; “Whiteness, Racism, and Identity” (2001); Racecraft: The Soul of Inequality in American Life (2012), with Karen E. Fields.
node.scope_note: The 1982 essay was not read on a permitted route; it is listed bibliographically only. The 1990 essay was read only through the publisher’s visible opening; interpretation beyond it is mediated by Johnson’s 2014 review. The 2001 essay was read only in abstract. Racecraft and Slaves No More were checked through publisher descriptions and, for Racecraft, Johnson’s review; neither book was read in full. Foner’s displayed 2022 review supports the graduate relationship; Cobb’s biography remains unread. Cited predecessors’ complete works remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Foner’s 2022 review of C. Vann Woodward: America’s Historian identifies Fields among Woodward’s former graduate students; Columbia dates her Yale doctorate to 1978.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author-posted review, lines 44–46: “former graduate students,” including Fields. Columbia education, line 92. Supports graduate training, without asserting agreement with every Woodward argument; Cobb’s book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Berlin and Fields coauthored Slaves No More (1992) with Steven F. Miller, Joseph P. Reidy and Leslie S. Rowland.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge author list and 1992 print date; description identifies “three essays.” Coauthorship only; individual essay allocation and whole-book reading are not claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Brute Ideology” (2014), Johnson uses Fields’s 1990 distinction between doctrine and ideology to question Davis’s interpretation of slavery.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author-posted PDF, p.131, paragraph beginning “In her classic 1990 essay”: “doctrine and ideology.” Fields’s original article beyond its publisher opening remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnson’s “Brute Ideology” (2014) praises Racecraft (2012) but questions its textual remedy and limited account of resistant political cultures.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author-posted PDF, pp.129–130 and 132: “corresponding narrowness” and “corrective.” Joint critique concerns Barbara and Karen Fields; book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Berlin, Miller, Reidy and Rowland, Fields’s Slaves No More (1992) places enslaved people’s actions at the centre of Civil War emancipation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge book description, first-essay paragraph: “place their liberty on the wartime agenda.” Read description, not essay body; collective argument and credit retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: In International Labor and Working-Class History's 2001 controversy 'Whiteness and the Historians' Imagination', Fields's 'Whiteness, Racism, and Identity' argues that whiteness as an organizing concept replaces racism with race and skirts the relations of power that placed African Americans in American society.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract: “replaces racism with race”; issue 60 controversy category. Abstract only; criticism addresses that approach within labour history, not the whole field or an inferred named opponent.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Labor in White Skin: Race and Working-class History” (1988), David Roediger criticised Barbara J. Fields’s “Ideology and Race in American History” (1982) for privileging class over race and underplaying Black nation-building in the formation of racial categories.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The body text addresses Fields’s argument over several paragraphs and supplies counterarguments about worker consciousness, African ethnic groups and nation-building. This is a substantive critique, not a claim of positive intellectual debt. The original year and essay identification are supplied by the publisher’s headnote and note 19 respectively.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Liberating Lincoln” (1994), James M. McPherson challenged Barbara J. Fields’s “Who Freed the Slaves?” (1990), arguing that emancipation remained reversible and depended on Union victory, Lincoln’s leadership and constitutional abolition.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: McPherson directly quotes Fields’s claim about the momentum of emancipation, rejects it, and discusses re-enslavement and the constitutional abolition of slavery. The review principally concerns books by other authors, so this records his substantive critique of Fields’s argument rather than treating it as a review of her book.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Slavery, Race and Ideology in the United States of America” (1990), Barbara J. Fields contributed to historical analysis of racial formation by arguing that legal and everyday practices continually reproduce American racial ideology.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The excerpt argues that the Supreme Court participates in practices that reproduce race and that historians must distance themselves from racial assumptions. Mapping this argument to the existing racial_formation endpoint is an editorial contribution classification; it asserts neither membership in Omi and Winant’s programme nor a debt to their work. No claim depends on the article’s unread remainder.
